extracted.intended_audience: journalists and newsroom editors reporting on crime and crime victims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters/editors on deciding what crime information to publish and how to report it to balance newsworthiness with victim protection and reduced bias. Covers identification, newsworthiness factors, harm-reduction practices, and anti-bias/dos-and-don'ts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance newsworthiness vs. harm (Core Tension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime might be newsworthy and the community should know — BUT reporting certain details might cause harm to victims or interfere with investigation/prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the public's need to know against potential harm to victims and possible interference with investigations or prosecutions. Treat newsworthiness as necessary but not sufficient justification for publishing details that could harm victims or investigative integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines on when to identify people involved in crimes (suspects, victims, witnesses, juveniles, family members).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally identify suspects after charges are filed. Sexual assault victims: typically NOT named unless they consent. Juveniles: typically NOT named (laws vary by jurisdiction). Domestic violence: protect identity. Witnesses: weigh safety vs. transparency. Family members of deceased: notify before reporting death. Apply local law and ethical considerations; prioritize safety and consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity of crime (newsworthiness factor)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the seriousness of the offense as a key factor in newsworthiness decisions; more severe crimes generally justify more detailed coverage, but severity alone does not override harm concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location / proximity to audience (newsworthiness factor)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents closer to the outlet's audience are more newsworthy; consider community relevance when deciding coverage level and detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity / prominence of victim or suspect (newsworthiness factor)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public figures or prominent community members increase newsworthiness; nevertheless protect non-consenting victims and avoid sensationalism tied to prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern or trend significance (newsworthiness factor)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an incident fits into a larger pattern or signals a trend, it has higher newsworthiness. Provide context and statistics rather than isolated anecdote reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police response significance (newsworthiness factor)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unusual, large-scale, or noteworthy police responses can justify coverage. Still evaluate how much detail is necessary and whether it jeopardizes investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community impact (newsworthiness factor)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the incident affects public safety, fear levels, or displacement in the community. Prioritize information that helps the public stay safe without inflaming fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice implications (newsworthiness factor)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories tied to trials, sentencing, or other justice-system milestones have news value; ensure accuracy and avoid conflating arraignment/charge with conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implications / calls for reform (newsworthiness factor)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an incident highlights policy failures or sparks reform debates, it merits contextual reporting that connects the event to systemic issues and potential solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-figure involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of a public figure increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When public figures are involved, the story may warrant broader or more detailed coverage, but reporters must still apply standards of accuracy, fairness, and harm mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of an investigative angle increases news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that allow deeper investigation (new information, patterns, institutional failures) justify more intensive reporting; ensure investigative methods don't retraumatize victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public safety implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the incident has immediate or ongoing public safety implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize information that informs and protects the public; avoid sensational details that elevate fear without adding useful safety information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual evidence availability (with care)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visuals can increase newsworthiness but require careful consideration to avoid victim identification, sensationalism, or privacy violations; do not publish graphic images gratuitously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolved vs. unresolved status
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the case is resolved or unresolved affects reporting decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unresolved or ongoing investigations may require withholding certain details to avoid prejudicing proceedings or endangering participants; update coverage as cases resolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anniversary / continuing significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Anniversary or continuing significance of an event raises newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories tied to anniversaries or long-term impact warrant reflective coverage that emphasizes context and avoids re-traumatizing victims with gratuitous detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-bias considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid disproportionate or biased coverage and provide context to prevent stereotyping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid disproportionate coverage of crime by minority groups; avoid over-emphasizing white female victims relative to underlying realities; provide context with statistics and trends; avoid mug-shot prominence for non-violent crimes; avoid publishing criminal-history details unless directly relevant; use neutral language. Proactively check for racial/ethnic representation biases in sourcing and imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm-reduction principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices to reduce harm to victims and sources when reporting crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show compassion to victims; be sensitive in approach; recognize emotional toll of repeated questioning; avoid graphic details when not necessary; update stories with positive outcomes; allow victim agency in the narrative (consent, control over identification). Use trauma-informed interviewing and limit retraumatizing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentencing Project: dos and don'ts (selected)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selected '10 Dos and Don'ts' for reporting on crime and victims from the Sentencing Project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DO contextualize crime statistics; DON'T generalize from single incidents; DO consider racial/ethnic representation; DON'T disproportionately use mug shots of people of color; DO interview reform advocates; DON'T center 'fear' framing; DO acknowledge structural causes; DON'T conflate suspects with convictions. Use these as concrete editorial checks on framing, sourcing, and imagery.
